articles.title: TRM-Raft: A Byzantine-Resistant Raft Consensus via Integrated Trust and Reputation Model
articles.excerpt: Internetware envisions autonomous software entities collaborating over the open Internet. Raft consensus is widely adopted for its simplicity and performance in distributed coordination, e.g., service registries and blockchains. However, Raft assumes crash faults only, making it vulnerable to Byzantine behaviors like election forgery and log tampering. Existing BFT protocols incur high overhead, while ad-hoc hardening lacks unified defense. We propose \textbf{TRM-Raft}, a Byzantine-resistant enhancement that non-intrusively integrates a Blockchain-based Trust and Reputation Model (B-TRM) into the consensus core. It quantifies multi-dimensional node behaviors, applies adaptive penalties distinguishing accidental faults from malice, and embeds reputation into leader election and log replication. A reputation-aware election penalizes term/index forgery, excluding low-reputation nodes from leadership. A Schnorr-signature-based mechanism lets followers verify log integrity; tampering triggers reputation decay and leader replacement. Evaluated on Hyperledger Fabric in a realistic Internetware setting, TRM-Raft keeps malicious leader ratio below 5\% even with 40\% Byzantine nodes, with <10\% throughput loss and <5\% latency increase over vanilla Raft. TRM-Raft offers a lightweight, practical trustworthiness path for Internetware systems relying on Raft.

articles.title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance
articles.excerpt: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 63.6% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 79.8% of runs containing violations. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.

articles.title: Empirical Limits of Risk-Averse Reinforcement Learning versus Gas-Aware Routing in Deterministic DeFi Execution
articles.excerpt: The migration of order execution to Automated Market Makers (AMMs) introduces two deterministic frictions absent from classical microstructure: closed-form constant-product slippage and Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) sandwich attacks gated by gas costs. We construct an end-to-end execution environment calibrated to live Uniswap V2 reserves, an EIP-1559 AR(1) gas process, and real Swap events, utilising stress-volatility gas shocks to make the MEV trigger informative. A Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) agent with a Rockafellar-Uryasev Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) penalty and a dual-head Chow-Ghavamzadeh critic is trained for one million steps across five risk-aversion levels and seeds, benchmarked against a myopic gas-aware oracle. We document a reproducible specification-gaming pathology: prior to a patch, a forced terminal liquidation routed through a no-MEV code path artificially inflated returns threefold and was preferentially exploited by higher-$\lambda$ runs. On the corrected environment, the strongest PPO variant captures 79\% of the myopic gas-aware oracle (46,542 $\pm$ 673 vs 58,786 $\pm$ 616 USDC), and extending the observation with three blocks of gas history fails to close the gap. We find no empirical evidence that the tested model-free MLP policies dominate this myopic gas-aware oracle, which can be evaluated in $\mathcal{O}(\log \epsilon^{-1})$ time per block. This result is robust to a $\sim$16x trunk-capacity expansion and a variance-controlled gas-history ablation. Code and reproducibility materials are available upon request.

articles.title: Reimbursement as a Revenue Instrument in Costly Clock Auctions
articles.excerpt: Bidders in an ascending auction may incur a cost each time they choose to continue, for example when bidding requires a blockchain transaction. We therefore investigate whether a seller can increase net revenue by reimbursing these costs, and how reimbursements should be distributed across auction rounds. We study auctions in which bidders must actively confirm their participation as prices rise and the seller commits to reimbursements before bidding begins. We first show how a linear program can find the cheapest payments that keep bidders' strategies optimal when participation costs are introduced. Maximizing net revenue, however, can require changing those strategies. In a two-bidder example, we identify conditions under which reimbursing only the last scheduled decision earns the most net revenue among the schedules we analyze. This policy outperforms no reimbursement, full reimbursement, and the cheapest policy that maintains the original strategies. Some auctions end earlier than under full reimbursement, but the seller's savings exceed the resulting loss in sale receipts. Experiments with learning bidders reproduce these revenue comparisons. In a four-bidder example, they also identify a policy with partial reimbursements in earlier rounds that earns more than reimbursing only the final decision. These results show how the seller's preferred reimbursement timing can change across auction environments. Finally, we explain how requiring bidders to confirm continued participation limits the prices they can be charged when messages are missing, and discuss the requirements for implementing these auctions on a blockchain.

articles.title: Sei Giga
articles.excerpt: We introduce the Sei Giga, a multi-concurrent producer parallelized execution EVM layer one blockchain. In an internal testnet Giga has achieved >5 gigagas/sec throughput and sub 250ms finality. Giga uses Autobahn for consensus with separate DA and consensus layers requiring f+1 votes for a PoA on the DA layer before consensus. Giga reaches consensus over ordering and uses async block execution and state agreement to remove execution from the consensus bottleneck.

articles.title: Multimmit: Low-Latency and Robust Transaction Ordering
articles.excerpt: To meet the throughput demands of blockchain systems, protocols for State Machine Replication increasingly have many processors disseminate transaction blocks in parallel. Certified designs require availability certificates before blocks enter the ordering process, which is robust but adds latency. BlueBottle, the leading uncertified design under $n\geq 5f+1$ ($n$ processors, at most $f$ Byzantine), reduces latency in favourable conditions but can put fetching missing data on the critical path. Raptr, the state of the art under $n\geq 3f+1$, avoids fetching on the voting path, but transactions wait for a leader's proposal and two voting rounds, and the leader controls the proposed sequence. We prove that strengthening the resilience assumption alone cannot remove Raptr's second voting round. We present Multimmit, a protocol for $n\geq 5f+1$ that builds on Raptr's approach and finalises leader blocks after a single round of voting, improving latency by at least one message delay. Extension votes let voters endorse fresh transaction blocks omitted from the leader's proposal: once a leader block finalises, every fresh, well-circulated block of an honest chain enters the total ordering by the next finalised leader block, even if that block's leader is Byzantine. Producer chains are interleaved by a prescribed rule, not in a leader-chosen sequence. Payments are final within a single round trip, once the producer assembles $n-f$ acknowledgments into a transferable receipt. With fifty validators across thirteen regions, Multimmit's median latency to placement in the total ordering moves from 383 to 411 ms as the offered rate rises from 100k to 1M transactions per second. At 100k, it is essentially unchanged under 0.1% message loss and rises by a factor of 1.4 with nine validators crashed; these conditions slow BlueBottle and Raptr, respectively, by more than an order of magnitude.

articles.title: fx(hash): Salvaging The Source Code of 28k Generative Artworks
articles.excerpt: fx(hash), the most radically inclusive generative art NFT platform, went bankrupt and shut down on August 17, 2026. The ownership of its 2,705,350 artworks is immutable on the Tezos and Ethereum blockchains, but the source code that generates them is off-chain and in peril. We salvaged all 28,193 generative programs contributed by 5,532 international artists and archived them in Software Heritage. Here we explain why NFT generative art is fragile and the steps we took to salvage these software cultural landmarks.

articles.title: PLATRS: A Lattice-Based Linkable Accountable Ring Signature for Permissioned Blockchains
articles.excerpt: Permissioned-ledger cross-domain data sharing needs anonymity and accountability: an endorsement hides its author, but a regulator must identify it on authorization reuse. Existing lattice-based schemes give these only separately: public traceability exposes signers to collision detectors; linkable non-tracing schemes cannot open; threshold schemes solve another problem. None gives post-quantum security, a signer-chosen ring, a publicly comparable per-event tag, and one-authority opening together. We propose \textsf{PLATRS}, a module-lattice linkable accountable ring signature for permissioned blockchains. Consortium-CA enrollment binds the key returned by an opening to a registered identity. The signer chooses the ring; verification is index-free; each signature has a per-event tag any verifier can compare. Tag noise derives from the signer's tracing secret and event, so linking is one comparison for honest signatures while the tag remains M-LWE without the secret. Detection is two-tier: tag mismatch is immediate; different tags on two accepted signatures for one event trigger an opening; the authority publishes the recovered public opening component, and any member recomputes the verdict against the ring. We prove CPA anonymity from M-LWE, linkability, authority-only traceability, and unforgeability from M-SIS with M-LWE in the random oracle model. At \(N=1024\), our open-source implementation: sign 9.886~ms, verify 3.919~ms, link 0.7~\(\mu\)s, open 480~\(\mu\)s; signature 107.3~KiB (log in ring size); adjudication 4.867~ms. Hyperledger Fabric: 60.5 signature submissions/s at 7.87~MB/s with 16~MiB blocks, commit-bandwidth limited. Common-harness: fastest of 5 schemes to sign/verify, second in size; vs FLLL\(^+\)21, signing is 3188\(\times\) faster and signatures 133\(\times\) shorter.

articles.title: zk-Agreements: A Privacy-Preserving Way to Establish Deterministic Trust in Confidential Agreements
articles.excerpt: Digital transactions currently exceed trillions of dollars annually, yet traditional paper-based agreements remain a bottleneck for automation, enforceability, and dispute resolution. Natural language contracts introduce ambiguity, require manual processing, and lack computational verifiability, all of which hinder efficient digital commerce. Computable legal contracts, expressed in machine-readable formats, offer a potential solution by enabling automated execution and verification. Blockchain-based smart contracts further strengthen enforceability and accelerate dispute resolution; however, current implementations risk exposing sensitive agreement terms on public ledgers, raising serious privacy and competitive intelligence concerns that limit enterprise adoption. We introduce zk-agreements, a protocol designed to transition from paper-based trust to cryptographic trust while preserving confidentiality. Our design combines zero-knowledge proofs to protect private agreement terms, secure two-party computation to enable private compliance evaluation, and smart contracts to guarantee automated enforcement. Together, these components achieve both privacy preservation and computational enforceability, resolving the fundamental tension between transparency and confidentiality in blockchain-based agreements.

articles.title: Do bid cancellations matter?
articles.excerpt: TL;DR. We ask whether proposers under ePBS will keep respecting bid cancellations, that is, signing each builder’s latest bid rather than the highest. We propose a common-value auction model and show that, if proposers can commit in advance to respecting or ignoring cancellations, this choice leaves expected proposer revenue unchanged and only shifts risk onto builders. Without commitment, however, respecting cancellations is not equilibrium behavior in the repeated game, since proposers gain from signing the highest bid. Using relay header logs, we find that this gain is small on average (0.9 ETH per day) but concentrated in volatile periods, and that some proposer setups already ignore cancellations, although we can detect this only in aggregate.
